Day 7 of GRC PULSE.

Search job listings for "GRC Professional" and you'll find almost none. Recent UK hiring data shows the actual titles doing GRC work are scattered — Analyst tops the list at roughly a quarter of roles, then Consultant, then Architect, Security Analyst, and Risk Analyst make up most of the rest.
That's not a data quirk. 

It reflects something true about the role itself: GRC isn't one job. It's a function that shows up inside a lot of different jobs.
So what does a GRC professional actually do, regardless of the title on the org chart?

They translate between languages that don't naturally understand each other. A security team talks in vulnerabilities and technical severity. Executives talk in budget and business impact. Regulators talk in specific legal requirements. A GRC professional is often the person who can hold all three conversations and connect them.
They ask uncomfortable questions early, instead of urgent ones late. Before a new vendor gets access to customer data, before a product launches, before a system goes live — the GRC professional is the one asking "what happens if this goes wrong, and are we allowed to do this."

They build and maintain the paper trail that proves things happened. Not because paperwork is the point, but because when a regulator, auditor, or customer asks "how do you know you're managing this risk," an answer without evidence isn't really an answer.

They don't own the risk. This one matters. A GRC professional identifies risk, assesses it, and helps decide how to treat it — but the actual risk belongs to the business function that created it. A GRC analyst flagging a vulnerability doesn't make the vulnerability their fault; it makes visibility their job.
Picture a mid-sized company rolling out a new AI vendor for HR data. The GRC professional isn't the one configuring the tool or negotiating the contract price. They're the one asking what data the vendor can access, whether that's covered under existing agreements, what happens if the vendor has a breach, and who signs off before this goes live.

The business impact of not having someone doing this work isn't always visible immediately. It shows up later — during an incident nobody assessed in advance, or an audit that surfaces a decision nobody can explain.

Practical takeaway: if your title doesn't say "GRC" but your job involves asking "are we allowed to do this, and can we prove it," you're already doing GRC work. The title catches up eventually. The function usually starts first.

A sudden 2x spike in job postings across major firms usually signals one thing. 
It is rarely just normal attrition. 
It points to a newly funded push, a major transformation project, or teams scaling up after a hiring freeze. 

When you see companies tripling their open roles overnight, the smartest move is not just throwing your resume into the portal. 
It is understanding why those roles exist and where your specific leverage lies. 

Here is how to approach high-growth hiring waves strategically:
1. Look past the volume and decode the operational need. 
A massive surge in enterprise hiring often points to scaling delivery challenges, route-to-market expansions, or large-scale digital transformations. 

2. Position yourself as an efficiency multiplier. 
In complex IT and go-to-market ecosystems, companies are not just looking for headcount. They want professionals who can design AI-powered automations, slash manual triage, and optimize workflows using LLMs and low-code tools. 

3. Speak the language of measurable impact. 
Whether you are managing global software programs, cutting support triage times by 60%, or negotiating multi-million dollar contracts, hiring managers want to see the bottom-line metrics behind your delivery. 

4. Leverage cross-functional alignment. 
Rapid scaling breaks silos. Highlight your experience in bridging pricing operations, IT, and external vendors to hit fixed delivery dates without friction. 

When the market accelerates, generic applications get lost in the noise. 

Targeted, value-driven positioning cuts straight through it.
